text: I would also ask for greater flexibility and compassion in assessing eligibility for various schemes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There are, understandably, criteria and rules in place to regulate the assessment.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, there may be situations where we need to exercise more discretion.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: She was eligible initially but had subsequently sold her flat as she was caring for her elderly mother and needed to liquidate some of her assets to pay for their expenses.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: She could not work as she was caring for her mother fulltime.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: She failed to note that selling her flat would make her lose her priority.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Her mother subsequently passed away and now she is hoping to stay in the same area as her sisters live there, too.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The chances of this happening are now much lower.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This may be a situation where some discretion could be exercised.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I appreciate that agencies do exercise discretion at times and accede to requests in various circumstances, and I hope that this approach is maintained and enhanced.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   Today, we are debating two Motions that call for a whole-of-Singapore effort to ensure that Singaporeans are able to age with purpose and dignity, and also to ensure support for caregivers is strengthened.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: When we speak of caregivers, it is important to ensure that any assistance rendered should also include caregivers to children and disabled adults.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: A host of challenges will certainly begin to occur when one reaches his or her golden years.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We have seen the advent of issues related to employment, housing, medical costs as well as caregiving.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am confident that with the combined efforts of the Government and Singaporeans, a comprehensive social support network can be created.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: (In Malay):   Sir, I would like to speak on three matters.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: First, I would like to request for the latest updates on Singapore's efforts to achieve the vision of "Successful Ageing for Singapore".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Second, I would like to ask MSF to conduct a study on issues related to our senior citizens, and the third matter is related to caregivers for the elderly.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The main task of this committee is to achieve the vision, that is, "Successful Ageing for Singapore".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The first report of this committee was published the following year in 1999.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This report covered various aspects of living that required transformation, enhancement and renewal in order to achieve "Successful Ageing for Singapore".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: These aspects of living were divided into three categories.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The first one is Heartware, which refers to the values, attributes and perceptions of the individual and society towards ageing and the elderly.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Second, Software, which encompasses national policies, plans and services that will provide opportunities and chances for our seniors to share and contribute their energy, experience and wisdom.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The third one is Hardware, that provides public infrastructure and facilities that are elderly-friendly so that it will be easier for them to interact and integrate with society.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: These three aspects of Heartware, Software and Hardware are essential in the effort to achieve Successful Ageing for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: To me, however, Sir, Heartware, which refers to society's values and attributes, is the main driver in shaping and creating a society that is highly concerned towards ageing issues.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: With the correct values and attributes, every individual will be involved sincerely and contribute as much as they can to make a concerted effort to achieve the vision that has been established.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, the process to transform values and attributes is admittedly not an easy one, as it takes time and requires continuous effort.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The first group comprises seniors who are still doing jobs like cleaning, collecting used utensils at the hawker centres and taking care of trollies.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The second group comprises seniors who collect cardboards, aluminium cans and other recycled material that are valuable enough to sell.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The question playing in everyone’s minds is why, at an age when one should be enjoying their retirement, there are still seniors like these who still have to sweat and toil and work hard.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Do they do this solely because they need to or because they want to?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: There are many views and perspectives on this issue.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Some say that these seniors do so because they require some pocket money, while others opine that it is an activity that fills up spare time and for recreation, and many also are of the view that these seniors do so in order to obtain some income to meet their daily basic needs.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Another issue that has often caught the people's attention in relation to our seniors is the issue of suicide.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: She also said that, with the increasing number of seniors in Singapore, it can be estimated that suicide cases among this group will continue to increase.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The task of caring for our seniors is undeniably a very challenging one, especially for those who are taking care of seniors with chronic health conditions, particularly those related to ageing like dementia and Alzheimer's Disease.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This Chamber has, on several occasions, spoken about ways to provide support for caregivers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Suggestions given include mandating eldercare leave for caregivers who are working.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For full-time caregivers, who usually are the seniors' own family members, it was suggested that CPF top-ups be given.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: It has been heartening to observe agencies from different sectors across the Government, arts and cultural companies and enterprises coming together to introduce a variety of arts and culture programmes for senior citizens, allowing our seniors to live a vibrant, meaningful and active life in their golden years.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Artistes and arts companies spare no efforts in staging concerts and play productions targeting our seniors.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Be it as an audience, volunteer, participant or mentor behind the scenes, our seniors are actively involved in the arts.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: More can be done to engage our seniors in arts.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Three in four seniors surveyed acknowledge the benefits of the arts, and value it as a means of inspiration, expression and bridging differences.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: They even developed a much more positive outlook in life which acts as a preventive measure for those who are diagnosed with depression and bipolar disorder.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: In relation to the survey, the NAC's signature Silver Arts Festival showcases the meaningful possibilities seniors have in and through the arts in their everyday lives.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The annual festival has engaged and attracted close to 40,000 seniors through music, film, theatre and more.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: NAC has also developed cross-sector partnerships with Social Service Organisations (SSOs), allowing beneficiaries within the social service sector to have increased access to the arts.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: This is made possible through initiatives like Art Reach and the WeCare Arts fund, a collaboration between NAC and PA.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: One of the recipients, Sri Warisan Som Said Performing Arts, has been working closely with our seniors, together with TOUCH Community Services.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: While we engage our seniors in the arts, we must also not forget to pay tribute to our seniors who are involved in the arts themselves as a mentor, teacher and practitioner artiste.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: They have dedicated their lives to the arts, enriching Singapore's cultural landscape.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: They now guide and nurture our next generation of artists in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: In addition to the NAC's efforts, there are also many national and local arts companies, such as the Esplanade, National Gallery, the Singapore Chinese Orchestra (SCO), Ding Yi Music Company, The Necessary Stage, Drama Box and Nam Hwa Opera, with the support from the corporate enterprises and foundations which are also engaging our seniors in their own ways with their respective programmes, workshops and initiatives.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The therapeutic and intrinsic values that the arts have on our seniors are something we have to reflect on, where the involvement of our elderly in the arts can help them enjoy a better quality of life and maintain a curious and active mind in their golden years.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that there will be more support and resources catered for our seniors from the Government across all sectors, more companies and enterprises, including the people and the public, and bringing and making the arts more accessible for our seniors across society, allowing our seniors to live with dignity, purpose and peace of mind in their golden years, leading a healthy, happy and gracious life.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: In recent years, various Government agencies, arts and cultural companies and enterprises have come together to introduce a variety of arts and cultural programmes for senior citizens, allowing our seniors to live a vibrant, meaningful and active life in their golden years.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Artists and arts companies are more willing to stage productions targeting our seniors.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: So, be it as an audience, volunteer or participant, our seniors can play an important role in these arts and the cultural activities.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Studies done by the NTU's School of Social Sciences and the NUS Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine found that participating in the arts or simply attending arts-related events can significantly increase the mental and physical health of our seniors.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: They can enjoy a higher quality of life and better physical and mental health compared to those not attending any arts and cultural activities.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: If seniors can actively participate in community or cultural events, their memory can be improved and dementia can be prevented.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister for Culture Community and Youth, Ms Grace Fu, pointed out at the Silver Arts Seminar on 6 September 2017 that there were many benefits for seniors to participate in arts activities.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Three in four seniors surveyed see arts as a channel to know people with different cultural backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: This survey affirmed our efforts to connect communities and encourage people to live a more meaningful life through arts and cultural activities.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: NAC's Silver Arts Festival held every September showcases a series of music, film, theatre events at multiple locations around the island.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Many of these events are free so that seniors can develop their arts potential through music, dance and other artforms, and have fun together with their family and friends.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: NAC has worked with many organisations, such as MOH, AIC, Singapore Mental Health Association and Singapore Dementia Association, to incorporate arts seminars and activities into the social services and health sectors, and to develop more support for arts.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: NAC will increase arts contact points in the community by bringing art performances to nursing homes and community hospitals.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: NAC will also train more cultural volunteers to hold arts events for seniors living alone.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: The flagship event is "Sing Out Loud", aimed to teach seniors with dementia to sing and take part in music activities.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: By doing this, seniors have one more channel to express themselves and they also have the opportunity to learn different vocal techniques when both their mind and body are being stimulated.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: For these seniors, this was their first time in life to step into the National Gallery where the beauty of the facade and the interior of the building have struck them deeply.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: SCO, Ding Yi Music Company, The Necessary Stage and the Nam Hwa Opera are doing their part to introduce arts to our seniors.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Nam Hwa Opera even brought Chinese opera to the various community hospitals, so that the seniors can watch the Chinese opera at close distance.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: These arts groups have their own regular workshops and performances to interact and build rapport with seniors.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: I hope the seniors can enjoy this golden moment of their life by embracing arts and exploring their potentials.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Through arts, they can build confidence, become more charming and reinvent themselves.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Here, I would like to commend the 125 Cultural Medallion recipients.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: They are the maestros in the artistic field and have been contributing passionately to the arts and cultural development in Singapore all their life.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Going forward, I hope the Government can put in more support and resources to develop arts activities for seniors, for example, introducing a Cultural Pass, to benefit more seniors.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: We also hope more Government agencies, enterprises and the people’s sector can join the efforts, use arts as a tool to bring people joy and exert influence and allow our seniors to live a happy, healthy and gracious life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This House has debated and endorsed numerous Motions and Bills in support of an ageing population in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Just last year, for instance, we debated a Private Member's Motion on support for senior citizens.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The importance of addressing the ageing issue in Singapore is clear and cannot be overstated.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Significant progress has also been made, with much being done to improve the physical infrastructure and social programmes benefiting our seniors by the Government.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Government spending has also increased by multiple folds.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Government has implemented comprehensive measures to support the ageing needs of our seniors in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is now time to also pay attention to caregivers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In MacPherson, I have met many caregivers of elderly residents.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These caregivers include elderly parents, children who are singles and siblings.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is a common sight that these caregivers give up their jobs and personal pursuits to care for their elderly loved ones.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The care demands are high, and they are often too absorbed with keeping up with their daily schedules to pay attention to what happens around them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: On Monday, I met a resident Chris at my weekly Meet-the-People Session.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Chris is in his early 30s and the sole caregiver of his father who suffers from dementia and is prone to falls.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Chris' mother passed away years ago after succumbing to cancer and his younger brother cannot be relied on as he had left the family.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As a result, Chris had to juggle working in the day and caring for his father at night.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As his father is prone to falls, Chris can hardly sleep every night as he stays alert to his father's movements.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: He must stay alert all the time; he cannot let up.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Chris was visibly burnt out when I saw him, a far cry from how he was years ago before his mother's demise.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: He is unable to perform at work, unable to get a good pay, unable to pay off his study loans, unable to afford a domestic helper.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: He is clueless about what he needs to do to care for his father properly and does not know what care options are available to them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I offered some suggestions to Chris and helped him write in to AIC to seek help.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Chris is perhaps considered to be better off than some of the other caregivers I have met in the community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At least, he still has a job and is young enough to cope with the physical demands of work and caring for his father.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But even so, he is burnt out and needs help.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Caregivers form an important pillar of support in our ageing landscape.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They are also critical in delaying potential institutionalisations, and enabling our aspirations of helping Singaporeans age in place.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, it is imperative that we strengthen our support to caregivers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Given my observations in the course of my constituency work in MacPherson, I have the following recommendations for the Government.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Whilst Chris is still able to fetch an income, many caregivers are not.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They gave up jobs to care fulltime for their elderly loved ones.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If they are fortunate, they may have savings or contributions from married siblings to rely on.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But savings can deplete quickly, and regular contributions are not guaranteed.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Others may have to apply for public financial assistance to cover basic living expenses.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But such financial assistance often does not cover other caregiving expenses.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Also, not every household wants to or can hire a foreign domestic helper to care for their elderly, as in the case of Chris.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second, enhance accessibility to care information, schemes and support services.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In my engagements with caregivers, many are often clueless about the types of help available and how to obtain them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Sometimes, when they need particular care information or apply for, say, motorised wheelchairs, they imagine themselves having to navigate various Government departments and filling in long questionnaires.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For others who are more digitally savvy and turn to the Internet for information, they dread having to trawl through different websites to piece together the information they need.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, access to care information, schemes and support services needs to be enhanced.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: AIC was announced as the one-stop agency for all elderly matters in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I voiced my support for this last year.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But more can be done to exploit its full potential.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Despite so much good work done, many of my elderly residents and their caregivers are not aware of the agency and what it is able to offer.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, we need to raise the awareness of AIC as the one-stop agency for information and assistance.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Similarly, digital options should also be made available and widely publicised to benefit caregivers who are digitally savvy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Third, respite care for caregivers beyond conventional working hours.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As in the case of Chris, he desperately needs a respite, especially at night, when he needs to rest and when his father who has dementia is active.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Chris was pale and drifting off at times during our conversation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I was worried and told him that even superheroes need a break.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: He agreed, but he asked, "Where and how to?” It was a good question.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I also meet elderly parents who are still struggling to care for their aged children suffering from mental disabilities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Physically washed out, but still pushing on because their love and sense of responsibility are too strong for them to let go.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To be ready for an ageing population and give support to caregivers, relying on the Government alone is not enough.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The society, too, needs to play a more active role.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Employers constitute a group of key stakeholders whose compassion and willingness to adapt working arrangements for workers who are caregivers as well are called upon.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the case of Chris, there is a limit to the number of leave days that he is entitled to.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: His father is generally fine in the day, as he is still physically fit and has a routine to follow.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But there were times when his father was hospitalised due to fall injuries or when he went missing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Upon utilising all his entitled leave days, Chris could resort to taking unpaid leave, but this is undesirable as this affects his income when he is already struggling financially.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Also, taking leave reduces his "face time" at work and affects his perceived work performance.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Chris is not alone in facing such a situation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Having sufficient leave days to care for an elderly loved one is much needed, but it is untenable over the longer term.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, I urge employers to keep an open mind, embrace FWAs where possible.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So far, we have seen encouraging results in terms of re-employment through the Re-employment Act and hiring of seniors through the Special Employment Credit.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Less face time does not mean less commitment to work.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Ensuring a fair appraisal will send a positive signal to all employees and enhance manpower retention as well as staff motivation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As Singaporeans live longer and work longer, we can expect more senior workers who are caregivers as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, FWAs and corresponding adjustments to appraisals to value quality over sheer quantity are increasingly imperative, and I call on employers to work with the Government to implement such arrangements.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So far, efforts have been focused on supporting seniors as care recipients.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It will be very sad if we are unable to take care of our seniors’ basic needs and it will reflect poorly on us as a civilised society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, we must be more optimistic and ambitious as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I have made this statement in this House before and I will repeat it, that I firmly believe that our seniors are much more capable than being mere recipients of care.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As we enhance our healthcare, we can expect longer and more healthy years.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As our economy evolves, there will be less reliance on physical strength at the workplace but more use of intellect and wisdom.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As each population becomes better educated and more savvy with the digital space, there will be less fear and deeper entrenchment of technology in our lives.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some hold the belief that you will get useless when you age.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: While I understand there are some constraints that come with age, I do not agree with this belief.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is self-defeating and we risk a self-fulfilling prophecy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to keep active and keep trying.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Of course, we hope we do not have to work into our old age because we have to, but I hope we can continue to contribute because we love to.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It brings meaning to life, and it helps us look forward to every new day with new hope.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, I call on all seniors to maintain a positive outlook and to lead an active lifestyle.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In reality, we know that it takes more than a willing senior to lead a successful active ageing lifestyle.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I made several calls on the Government in this House before to create favourable conditions for our seniors to age actively and gracefully.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Allow me to reiterate some of them here.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: First, create a favourable environment and employment opportunities for seniors who want to work.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Government can take the lead in testing how work environment, workflows, job role designs and even compensation and benefits, such as health benefits, can be optimised for senior workers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second, create meaningful volunteering opportunities that play to the strength of our seniors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I was especially struck by an example of this lady called Mdm Anne Choo when I attended the opening of the Brahm Centre in December last year.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At the centre, we were introduced to Mdm Choo, who, despite being in her late 70s, almost 80, is still very active.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: She turned from being a volunteer to a staff with the Brahm Centre, and every day she would visit the elderly, some of whom might be younger than her, visiting them, encouraging them, and helping them through with physiotherapy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: She is an inspiration and, to be honest, after hearing her story, she is my dream, and I hope that one day when I grow old, I can be like her.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Understand the physical requirements and cognitive characteristics of seniors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Apply elder-friendly designs into our hardware and heartware solutions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to mainstream elder-friendly designs and make them pervasive.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to apply elderly-friendly designs to the development of common spaces, facilities, machine interfaces, workflows, public processes, smart phone applications and more.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Equip seniors with the tools and know-how so that they can access the Internet and take advantage of useful mobile applications.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Help them harness technology to stay connected to news and information, support networks and friends and families.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In Mandarin):   There is a saying that goes like this, "the young should not mock the old, for there will be a day when he himself will age as well." This is a very interesting statement, and I have two interpretations for that.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: After all, we will all age one day.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If we do not respect and take care of the elderly today, who will respect and take care of us when we get old?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Being old does not mean that one is useless and will be detested.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Just like sunset, the elderly, too, can cast a beautiful glow in their old age.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Population ageing in Singapore is a familiar topic to us.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For years, the Government has been making tremendous efforts to tackle the challenges brought forth by ageing and seeking ways to better take care of the elderly.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The result is clear to all, especially when it comes to elderly welfare, which has been put in place gradually.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But at the same time, as we tackle the challenges brought forth by ageing and strive to fulfil the vision of ageing in place, we cannot neglect the important role played by caregivers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to take care of their welfare as well and give them practical support.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In community service, we often see that many of these caregivers are actually family members of the elderly.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They take pains to take care of the elderly.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some even give up their careers and dreams.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In this process, they will encounter many difficulties and need assistance.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As such, I hope that the Government can be more proactive and provide more comprehensive support to the caregivers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To implement FWAs, the performance appraisal system should also be tweaked to pay more attention to quality of work.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is not only fairer, but also more humane.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To the employees, it is also a form of encouragement.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Lastly, I would like to encourage everyone to support active ageing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We should not have this negative mindset that "being old is useless", because the elderly can also lead a vibrant life, like a beautiful sunset.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Even in our twilight years, we can still strive to broaden our horizons, keep up with new trends, continue to learn, enjoy ourselves and contribute to the society.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As our society ages, the role of caregivers becomes ever more critical as they help our seniors age with purpose and dignity, in particular, those who need assistance for their day-to-day activities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Caregivers perform a multitude of tasks, including providing personal care, arranging for transportation and medical care as well as performing tasks inside and outside the home.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They can be divided into two broad categories, namely, professional caregivers and informal caregivers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They take care of our family members and enable us to continue working.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They enable Singaporeans to pursue their careers knowing that their loved ones are in good hands at home.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To attract and retain professional caregivers, it is important to ensure that professional caregivers have the opportunity for career progression and timely wage adjustments that are commensurate with their skillsets and experience.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Relevant and continued training is also necessary to ensure their knowledge is regularly updated to enable them to provide better care to those entrusted to them.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I believe that we can, and must, do more to recognise and support our caregivers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are four important components to the PWM: career progression, wages, skills and productivity.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Being a professional caregiver requires passion and dedication.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But caregivers face tremendous stress in carrying out their work, and the possibility of getting emotionally drained at the end of a day is real.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Alongside good career progression, it is also important to have strong support groups to care for our caregivers, too.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, I want to touch on support for informal caregivers, who are commonly referred to as home caregivers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These are individuals who have not undergone any formal training on caregiving, nor are they being paid for providing care to their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These individuals often have to juggle their caregiving roles with a full-time or part-time job.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a society, more can be done to help them.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We can provide better support for caregivers in three areas, namely, workforce support, community support and technological support.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Employers need to recognise that, in an ageing society, their employees will need to attend to elderly family members more and more.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Currently, some employers have implemented initiatives, such as parent care leave.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, these are usually limited to just two days a year.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I urge employers to provide more flexibility in granting parent care leave.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Employers should also embrace FWAs and allow their employees with caregiving needs to be able to work from home.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Another area of workforce support is supporting caregivers' re-entry into the workforce.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some home caregivers have had to take a few years off their careers to provide care to their loved ones, and it can be challenging to re-enter the workforce with a gap in between jobs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can the Government do more to facilitate their re-entry into the workforce?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Perhaps, given their experience in caregiving, we can help ease them into the professional caregiving sector.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This can also address the local manpower crunch in the industry.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The community plays an important role in supporting caregivers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Monfort Care's Yishun Centre provides caregivers and their elderly with free hand massage and complimentary coffee and tea at their centre.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: During the interactions, volunteers at the centre also help keep a lookout for the well-being of the caregivers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Last month, a cancer support group "Never Alone" was launched, creating a platform for cancer survivors to share their experience with other cancer patients.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They bring hope to those who are struggling with their illness and also increase confidence that they are not alone in their journey.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the same way, caregivers need to know that they are not alone.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This brings me to my third point on technological support.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Last year, the "Dementia Friends" app was launched to help caregivers of dementia patients alert others when their loved ones go missing, so that others using the app can help keep a lookout for the missing person.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The app also provides useful information for caregivers, such as the importance of self-care.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Such apps are useful and should be extended to other medical conditions, such as stroke, diabetic and end-stage cancer.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With technology, we can build a virtual community of support for caregivers who often feel isolated in their caregiving roles.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Through the online platform, bite-sized training may be uploaded for the caregiver to learn from professionals and others.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This would help address the common feedback that caregivers do not have time to attend formal training.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some of us will have the fortune to be surrounded by our loved ones who will take care of us no matter what, be it to take on an informal caregiving role, or to hire a professional caregiver.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some, however, will be admitted to a nursing home due to various personal and family circumstances.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The current model requires bidders to compete primarily on price.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But this is an unsustainable race to the bottom.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Even before that happens, the current funding model already requires our nursing homes to stretch every dollar today.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is not difficult to imagine how a lack of funds can affect the service standards at our nursing homes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With our rapidly ageing population, more can be done by all stakeholders – employers, the Government, the community – to enhance support to caregivers, and to help our seniors age with purpose.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, I would like to thank my Parliamentary colleague, Mr Melvin Yong, for mentioning the Goodlife!@Yishun and Cancer Support movement in Nee Soon South.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, on this note, I would like to thank all those supporters who have contributed generously.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In this House, we want to help every Singaporean lead a happy and fulfilling life.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As Singaporeans live longer, they spend an increasing proportion of their lives as senior citizens, or caregivers to senior citizens.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, it is timely that we look at how to help Singaporeans spend their silver years happily.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: My colleagues have been speaking about several priorities, including employment and volunteering opportunities for the elderly and helping caregivers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Employment and volunteering opportunities are important because many elderly still have a lot to give.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They want to feel useful to society in a way that is manageable for them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If they have a purpose, it will help stave off issues, such as dementia, depression and so on.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is popular with the general public while also being a space for seniors to pursue activities, such as arts, model-making, reading and so on.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Seniors who work there are paid a small sum, but their biggest takeaway is actually the experience.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: By working there, they have a sense of purpose and community.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And they can connect with customers of different ages who come into the café.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Similarly, at the Goodlife!@Yishun centre, on the other side of the road, we have a small café.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Elderly volunteers brew the coffee and tea and make food there together.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Anyone passing by can drop in to have some coffee and tea for free.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is when the Montfort Care staff can chat with them, find out if they have any needs and involve them in the centre's activities for the elderly and caregivers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Elderly volunteers also run outreach and activities at the centre and the community.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The costs are quite minimal, covered by paying customers or donors.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I would urge my colleagues to work with the VWOs in your area and look into similar models.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The aromatherapy and massage are done by volunteers, some of whom are our elderly residents that we have trained.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The sensory therapy can help caregivers to relax and destress.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But also, volunteers can take the opportunity to uncover issues the caregivers may be facing.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This way, we can identify problem areas early and step in to give assistance.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The centre also offers respite to caregivers and support groups for caregivers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Another thing we are doing for caregivers is promoting a dementia-friendly community.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We know it can be very stressful to care for a dementia patient, especially if the patients have to be watched over all the time.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We want to build a community where dementia patients can continue to go to the coffee shop or market like they have always done.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This will enable them to age in place and also slow the onset of dementia.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It will also give caregivers some peace of mind.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We have found that senior citizens have a lot to give.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They can look after themselves, help other elderly and be the glue that holds the community together.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: With the help of HPB, we have exercise classes in every RC, every Neighbourhood Committee (NC), every park, every pavilion and every condominium.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In Springleaf Estate alone, there are 14 different exercises and the residents are very active.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They bring their family members, neighbours and friends.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And besides exercises, they also learn new hobbies from fellow residents.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, our elderly residents go out of their homes more often, make more friends and they become happier residents.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: On this note, I would like to thank HPB for bringing such good programmes and doing great work.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: At the part of Nee Soon South, a group of senior residents started community gardening in Zone F.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Every time after each harvest, they will be lugging the vegetables, crossing Yishun Avenue 4 to Zone H and they donate the vegetables to the Community fridges meant for residents in the rental blocks.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These senior residents are the ones with the golden heart.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What they need is just the right support.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I urge my colleagues to share what they are doing in their constituencies.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We are very fortunate to live in Singapore.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We have a good Government which works tirelessly for its people.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope our businesses, each and every individual, can do our part and help to build the other heartware.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In this way, our senior citizens will enjoy their old age to the fullest.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   Today, we are talking about how to help our senior citizens to truly age with dignity.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The programmes we introduced in Yishun South perhaps can offer some ideas.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Near the Khatib MRT station, there are two cafes, both manned by seniors.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: One of them is, in fact, an SAC.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This service and other outreach activities are all conducted by senior volunteers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Through these programmes, we discovered that the seniors can contribute a lot to the society.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that the other Members of Parliament can share the experience in your constituencies, so that we can learn from one another.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In Singapore, we are fortunate we have a very good Government which is always concerned about the welfare of the people, which works tirelessly for its people and provide us with good hardware and infrastructure.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope our businesses, and each of us will work together with the Government to make Singapore into a beautiful island with good hardware and heartware, whether in terms of money or time.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In this way, our senior citizens will live more happily, comfortably and age in place.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With increasing life expectancy and decreasing birth rates, there will be more elderly people and we must change our mindset to see ageing as a new stage of opportunity and strength.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As a society, we must create an environment where Singaporeans can age with purpose and dignity.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many of our elderly workers put in long hours of manual labour every day and need their breaks.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Ideally, they would spend this time in a proper rest area where they may have their lunch, or just sit down, catch their breath, and find some peace amidst a long, gruelling day.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Unfortunately, there is a glaring absence of proper rest areas in many buildings, especially for outsourced workers who are cleaners, security officers and landscape workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But there are steps we can take to improve this.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And we all have a part to play.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With part of the cost managed, building owners will be more inclined to implement this for their outsourced workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Such rest areas will go a long way in improving their working conditions.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: No longer do they have to find secluded corners or staircases to have their breaks.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They can have a greater sense of dignity and self-worth knowing that their basic needs are provided for at their workplace.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There are also tripartite standards on Age-friendly Workplace Practices, jointly developed by MOM, NTUC and the Singapore National Employers Federation.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Employers can refer to this to create age-inclusive work practices.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The new standard will create an environment conducive for older Singaporeans to work as long as they are willing and able to, in jobs that are safer and smarter, and in a work environment where they feel valued and their needs are addressed.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Start by ensuring all workers, including those elderly workers, are properly trained and familiar with work safety and health practices.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Employers can also invest in technology to make their work easier and safer.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As an individual, we can be more considerate to make the work easier for our elderly workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Simple gestures like returning trays at the hawker centres, greeting them and saying "thank you" can make a lot of difference to these workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Let them know that their work is appreciated.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Let them know that they are not invisible.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And these workers can age knowing that they have a purpose in life.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At the end of the day, we will all grow older.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Would we not all want to age with respect and dignity?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Let us treat our elderly the way we would like to be treated when we are old.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   There are many seniors amongst us who work in the cleaning and security sectors.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Break times are usually allocated for them but, unfortunately, no suitable rest areas are provided at their workplace.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I feel sad whenever I come across elderly workers who have to take their breaks in a remote corner or have to simply sit at the common staircase area.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is important that we take care of the welfare of our seniors who are still working.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe that a suitable rest area can make these elderly workers feel that their work is appreciated, and they will be grateful because we recognise them as workers who deserve to be treated fairly.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, I support both Motions.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Many of them require help in navigating where to get help, where to obtain financial and workplace support, empowerment and training services.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Whilst the Parliamentary Motion relates mainly to caregivers of seniors, I would like to focus on one unique group of caregivers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These are the caregivers of persons with disabilities (PWDs), mostly parents who are themselves ageing.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These unique caregivers face the double whammy of dealing with (a) their own ageing and (b) the ageing of their children with disabilities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In 2014, it was reported in local news that the mother of a child with special needs threw him out of their HDB flat, causing his death.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The mother, his caregiver, had developed major depression and was seized by the thought that the son was the cause of her misery.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Amongst the thousands of caregivers I have met, there are some, however, who are so willing to give of themselves that they put their child’s interest way above their own.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: She has two severely disabled children in their late 30s whom she serves, lifts, feed throughout the day.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The last I saw her at the house visit, she was exhausted and obviously physically challenged due to the heavy lifting that she does each day looking after her adult disabled children.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Another resident of mine, Mr Lim, not his real name, in his 70s, is a single parent looking after his severely autistic son who is also in his 30s.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: When Mr Lim fell ill and could not care for his son, the son was sent to IMH for a period, causing great grief to Mr Lim who pleaded for his return.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Mr Lim felt he could not even afford to fall sick.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Then, there is another group with whom I have had the opportunity to serve.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These are parents who are able and willing to not only provide for their own children but also use their professional skills to build services and programmes in VWOs for disabled children of others.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But whoever they are, one common denominator remains.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For every one of these parents I know and every parent I meet at many focus groups, all of them worry over what will happen to themselves and to their adult children when they themselves lose their mental capacity or pass on.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Hence, I urge the Ministry to engage, facilitate and communicate regularly to the special needs community the progress of the Masterplan and to finetune the plan as developments occur.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: With that in place, the adoption of a systems approach to address the needs of this unique group of caregivers of PWDs would be very useful.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Hence, I propose five steps in a systemic approach of identifying, individualising, integrating, implementing and inspecting the support process of this group of caregivers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The attempt to develop nationwide databases of persons with disabilities and their caregivers has not been very fruitful due mostly to a lack of resolve and organisation.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, at the local neighbourhood level, it is highly possible to tap on the current services rendered by organisations, such as the Silver Generation Office, SSOs and grassroots organisations, a local infrastructure, to develop local databases to identify and locate this group of caregivers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Every family is different in needs, abilities and fortitude.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some lack skills, money or other resources to effectively plan and organise the care for their loved ones.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some are positive and caring while others are negative and unconcerned.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In our attempt to strengthen caregiver support in our country, we must beware of the cookie-cutter solutions that do not address the individual family situation.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Depending on their abilities – whether in finance or skills – and willingness, the needs of these caregivers can occur on a continuum, and the level of support should be matched to those needs and their changing nature over time.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some caregivers are able and willing, and what they require are regular updates and menu of services they can tap on.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some caregivers are able but not willing, and they will need engagement and coaxing to do their part.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some are willing and not able and will need to be trained and equipped.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Others who are neither able nor willing will require other forms of support.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The need for a systems integrator, although it is a term that is usually used in the commercial sector or computer sector, it is also a term that is very useful in the social service sector.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The need for a systems integrator to facilitate the case management or equipping others to integrate the various needs and solutions cannot be underestimated.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, SGE will need to be resourced much more to reach out to many more, beyond its physical premises, and to play the role of an effective integrator or to train others to be effective integrators to facilitate the systems approach I am advocating.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And the last step is really – inspect.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The process of caregiver support is an ongoing one and needs and commitment level can change over time.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, tracking and inspection are one of the very key steps to ensure that this systematic and systemic approach of caregiving support is done.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, in conclusion, Speaker, Sir, the role of a caregiver is a challenging one with multiple stress points.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to declare my interest as the Immediate Past President and current member of the Society for WINGS, an Institution of Public Character (IPC) and registered charity that empowers women to age well.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It has been said that there are only four kinds of people in the world: those who have been caregivers, those who are currently caregivers, those who will be caregivers, and those who will need a caregiver.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, I was recently at a corporate event and met a most unlikely caregiver, Siti, a young professional in her 20s who became emotional when sharing her caregiving challenges with her three unmarried aunts in their 60s – one suffering from diabetes and depression, another from ovarian cancer and the third from kidney failure.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, this role is, ironically, one of the most undervalued in our society.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The psychosocial well-being of caregiving must be top of mind for our caregiving policies, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We have not done a comprehensive national study on caregiver health, which I highly recommend we do.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: But segmented studies revealed that our caregiver population is certainly facing increasing risk with their mental health.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: A study by IMH in 2017 noted a pooled prevalence rate of 40.2% for depressive symptoms among caregivers of stroke survivors.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet another study found that caregivers of cancer patients are at greater risk of developing depression than the general population.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Wendy is one such caregiver who was a respondent to a study by the Association of Women for Action and Research (AWARE) on the financial cost of caregiving.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: She is 51 years old, single, and caregiver to her mother who has dementia.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: She hired an FDW to help with caregiving, yet is the "emotional anchor" for her mother.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Caregiving has taken a toll on Wendy emotionally, physically and financially.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: She has had panic attacks and experiences high levels of anxiety.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Then, there is Ivan, in his 50s, who is struggling to cope with the severe care needs of his 85-year-old mother, also suffering from dementia.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Unable to deal with his mother's mounting behaviour issues last year, he had a series of anxiety attacks and ended up in hospital himself.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We all know that with smaller families, there are fewer family caregivers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Over the past few decades, however, Singaporeans have been fortunate to have an army of efficient, dedicated and relatively affordable FDWs.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: They form an important part of our informal care workforce.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, the same Duke-NUS study found that, I quote, "families who hire domestic helpers are also not necessarily able to relieve this mental stress.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, some feel that having domestic help increases this stress.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: About half of the respondents polled hire domestic helpers and, of these, about 55% of the domestic helpers do not have experience caring for the elderly or have received training in doing so." Mr Speaker, the economic impact of caregiving on the caregiver and Singapore is obvious.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This number does not include caregivers who have had to scale back on work commitments in other ways, for example, by moving to part-time or other work.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Wendy, whom I mentioned earlier, scaled down on her working hours and now earns less than $2,000 a month, about one-fifth of what she used to earn.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Ivan quit his job to look after his mother, after she repeatedly forgot to turn off the gas at home.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Another caregiver, June, stopped working completely when her husband was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: She is 60 years old and the sole caregiver to her husband as they have no children.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Their only monthly household income of $1,000 comes from renting out a room in their HDB flat.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Did these caregivers lessen their caregiving burden with formal care services?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Wendy tried daycare but her mother reacted violently against it.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: She is now considering the nursing home option, but the guilt is immense and she has been putting it off despite her own deteriorating emotional and physical health.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Then there is the cost of nursing home fee that she will struggle with to afford because of her drastically reduced income.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: June's husband goes to daycare, but she holds much guilt because he does not like it there.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, she needs that time to go to the hospital gymnasium to exercise her knee.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: June spends around $300-$400 on daycare, after Government subsidies, plus $100 on transport to her husband's daycare a month against her $1,000 rental income.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, in consideration of caregiver health, the increasingly complex care needs of our seniors and shrinking families, formal home-based and community care services are a critical and practical necessity.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: While the Government has been busy increasing capacity in recent years, more needs to be done to improve affordability and quality of these services.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Costs may, therefore, deter even middle-income families from using formal long-term care services, especially since many find it cheaper to hire an FDW instead.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, FDWs, and even family caregivers themselves, may not be trained enough to handle complex care needs and, sometimes, could end up compromising the well-being and health of vulnerable seniors, leading to unnecessary hospital stays.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Homecare is expensive, too, and appears underfunded with charity dollars, even after accounting for Government subsidies.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: While the CareShield Life insurance scheme will undoubtedly be useful, given the strict eligibility criteria and that the scheme is optional for older cohorts, how many will join remains to be seen.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Even as we work out ways to improve affordability, emphasis must be made on quality and outcomes.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In recent years, many sophisticated new care models, such as the Integrated Home and Daycare Programme, have sprung up.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Anecdotal evidence shows that these schemes are good at enabling seniors to be cared for well in the community.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, in order to convince sceptical caregivers of the effectiveness of these programmes, outcomes should be tracked and made public.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We have a largely healthy population and there has been considerable focus in recent years on harnessing the blessings of longevity.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, we can, and we should do more.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The spend in the last two years is not yet available.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Government should consider recalibrating the healthcare budget to enable seniors to age and be cared for at home.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: More subsidies can be targeted at seniors who are not severely disabled and, therefore, do not qualify for ElderShield or CareShield Life, but likely to benefit from professional rehabilitative care.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: To better support caregivers' psychosocial well-being needs, the Government can consider giving seniors flexible care packages for families to use as they wish, whether for daycare, homecare, respite care services, transport fees and consumables or to pay a family member or friend for elder-sitting.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Respite care should be enhanced to an integrated approach to include counselling and selfcare training services as well while keeping their aromatherapy and massage services.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Another way forward is to accord the long overdue recognition and appreciation to family caregivers with an allowance or payment, in both cash and CPF credits.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This also ensures some level of financial security for them.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The payment should vary by the number of ADLs the care recipient requires assistance with.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: And allow it to be used for the care of any family members, including older relatives.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, employers should be made a partner in this effort to provide FWAs on request by employees as well as consistently value the caregivers within their organisations through awareness and appreciation efforts.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Speaker, we should collectively embrace caregiving not as the burden of a few, like Wendy, June, Ivan or Siti, but a responsibility of all.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: There is an urgent need for more informed collective conversations among Singaporeans about what kind of care system we want for our grandparents, our parents – and eventually ourselves – and how much we are willing to pay for it, whether through premiums and/or taxes, for those who can afford it and to support those who cannot.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Because, Mr Speaker, to care for those who once cared for us is one of life’s highest honours.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: At the recent Future Jobs, Skills and Training Forum organised by NTUC, I met Mr Harbhajan Singh, who is an inspiring role model of active and productive ageing in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Mr Harbhajan is 78 years old, but age does not stop him from contributing his experience, skills and expertise as a Senior Nurse Manager and Emeritus Fellow at Tan Tock Seng Hospital.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In fact, at the age when most have retired, Mr Harbhajan, at 63, was on the frontline when the severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) hit Singapore, applying his almost 40 years of nursing experience in battling the communicable disease and caring for SARS patients.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Now at 78, Mr Harbhajan says that as long as he can still contribute, he will keep working at Tan Tock Seng Hospital.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Indeed, our mature workers, who are able and want to continue to contribute in the workplace, are treasure troves of experience and expertise, and more must be done to ensure that they are not overlooked or passed over due to ageist perceptions and discrimination.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I have three observations from the recent MOM Labour Market Advance Release 2018 and MOM's Report on Labour Force in Singapore 2018.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Forty-five percent of residents who were outside the labour force in 2018 were aged 60 and over.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: These residents who are outside the labour force could be a potential source of labour, given the right conditions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Higher skilled, middle-aged PMETs, being deemed too costly to retain and perceived as too old to be hired, are the hardest hit and most vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Three, while the non-seasonally adjusted unemployment rate for PMETs decreased for the second successive year to 2.9% in 2018, from 3% a year ago, older PMETs continue to face greater difficulty in the job market.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The long-term unemployment rate for resident PMETs aged 50 and above was at 1.5%, higher than the younger age groups, reflecting greater difficulties faced by older jobseekers in securing employment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I am concerned and worried that this may be exacerbated by the structural challenges in the labour market.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: To encourage active and productive ageing in the workplace, especially in our tight labour market where it is imperative that we maximise our human capital potential to secure Singapore’s competitiveness, all stakeholders have to take a harder look at the areas of work, workplaces and workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Employers need to look beyond stereotypes and ageist perceptions and see the value of mature workers to draw out this group’s fullest potential in their organisations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This group of workers not only have extensive work experience, but they are also likely to have a strong understanding of the organisation after many years with the organisation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Workers in the older age brackets are more likely to have worked at least 10 years in their current job.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In the same vein, they would also have strong and deep domain expertise and are gems for adjacent and new sectors as well as startups.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Employers must recognise that the growing pool of experienced and skilled mature employees in Singapore can help them maintain a competitive edge in the market.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: To encourage employers to see the value of mature workers, the tripartite partners and industry stakeholders must continue to build on the close partnerships to support mature workers through the advocating and adoption of fair employment practices to ensure those mature workers are not subject to discrimination in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: At the same time, the following existing schemes aimed at raising older workers' employability, which are coming to an end in 2019, should be enhanced and extended.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First introduced in 2011 to raise the employability of older Singaporeans, the SEC today provides a wage-offset to employers to hire Singaporean workers aged 55 and above and earning up to $4,000 a month.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Two, the Career Support Programme (CSP) is coming to an end on 31 March this year.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The CSP encourages employers to hire Singaporean PMETs aged 40 years and above who have been laid off or have been unemployed and actively looking for work for six months or more.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We must continue to upskill our mature workers, in tandem with industry and business transformation, to enable them to keep pace with the new and in-demand skills in their respective industries.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While the training participation rate for our resident labour force for those in the 50-64 age group has increased from 33.7% in 2017 to 40% in 2018, the participation rate in this age group is the lowest compared to the younger groups of workers as the perceived returns on training for this group is lower.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
