text: Employers can do more to provide our older workers with training opportunities at the workplace to enhance their productive longevity in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As our industries transform, the half-life of skills is decreasing.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Workers, including our mature workers, need to constantly upskill and reskill to stay relevant and employable and must be willing and open to explore new career opportunities.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Workers can take charge of their skills development and lifelong learning by tapping on their SkillsFuture Credits which were introduced in 2016.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As we encourage workers to adopt lifelong learning, it is timely for a top-up of the SkillsFuture Credits now so that workers, especially our mature workers, can take charge of their learning in pursuit of their personal growth.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Our workplaces must be age-friendly to allow our mature workers to continue to contribute as they progress in their years.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Employers need to redesign jobs and adapt workplace practices to take into consideration the needs of our older workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Under the current WorkPro programme, we have seen real-life examples of how employers have redesigned jobs to reduce labour-intensive processes to make the job more age-friendly for mature workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: These improvements are a win for both the employer and workers as business productivity is also raised through the job redesign.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The Work, Workers and Workplaces which I have mentioned are interdependent and must be looked into and addressed in a holistic manner.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We must also recognise that efforts to support active and productive ageing in the workplace must be made in parallel with efforts to improve the lived experience of older Singaporeans, such as through measures to help them to age healthily, age well, and have adequate resources to enable them to pursue their aspirations in their golden years.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The recommendations of the Tripartite Workgroup must address the multifaceted aspirations, challenges and needs of our older Singaporeans holistically to enable our older Singaporeans to age with purpose and dignity.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As we push on with efforts to build an age-friendly and age-inclusive workforce and society, I would like to end off with a quote from Mr Harbhajan, as he shares how being able to contribute and learn through his work enables him to age with dignity and purpose and the value of having an age-diverse workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: He says, "I feel healthy because I am working.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I come to work, meet people, socialise with them, I do tasks assigned to me and fulfil my function.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The knowledge I have can be used to guide the next generation of nurses and benefit them.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: At the same time, I also learn from them.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We must go on with continuing our education.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I have advocated the same in a speech I made during the debate on the Annual Budget Statement in April 2016.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I support the recommendation that the employer's CPF contribution rate for workers who are between 55 and 60 should remain at 17%.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I have to declare my interest in this relatively sensitive topic of CPF for older workers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: As a senior management staff of a large corporation, I would be very concerned with the ballooning wage costs if we were to increase the employer's CPF contribution rate for older workers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, we have to be objective to look at what is best for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Will employers start to replace older workers above 55 by large numbers due to the increase in CPF contributions?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: With the current tight labour market situation and an ageing population, it will be hard for companies to find younger workers to replace those above 55 in large numbers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Will employers start to consciously avoid employing older workers with the increase in CPF contribution rate?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Most of the time, job skill, job fit and the potential contribution of employees are much more important contributing factors in the hiring decision.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: CPF contribution is not the decisive factor most of the time.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In fact, with medical and technical advancements, changes in our lifestyle and greater reliance on knowledge workers rather than blue collar workers, the 50s today are our new 40s.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: From the perspective of older employees, the increase in employer's CPF contribution will mean a great deal.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: They will have more money to pay for the housing mortgage, more money to pay for their children’s tertiary education, more money to pay for their MediShield Life, CareShield Life and more.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Nonetheless, we still need to balance the interest of employers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Next, I would like to touch on how to better engage the seniors as they age.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: PA has been doing a good job in organising social activities for the elderly, like brisk walking, craft activities, mass dancing and outings like festive shopping, for example.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, I have observed that most of the time, 80% of those taking part in these social activities are women.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, I see many elderly man drinking coffee at coffee shops.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I see many elderly man playing chess games while drinking beer.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Although women live longer, but the average life expectancy of man has also increased from 65 in 1965 to about 80 today.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Thus, it is important that elderly men, especially after they have retired from their jobs, are socially engaged in healthy pursuits with their friends and kakis.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: As a Town Council Chairman, I have started to engage elderly men who are willing to help to inspect the estate for cleanliness, assist in light maintenance work, repairs or simple jobs like changing of light bulbs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: He moves around fixing broken locks, patching corroded cement surfaces and so on.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Rather than activities which revolve around social gathering and chit-chat, it may be more useful to come up with "work-based" activities, as men identify with their work or careers much more than women.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It is also good to look at what other countries are doing to engage the elderly men.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For instance, we could consider the example of Australia, the UK and the US where they have a "Men's Shed" movement.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Their slogan is "Shoulder to Shoulder", shortened from "Men don't talk face to face, they talk shoulder to shoulder", which says a lot about how we should engage elderly men.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Men’s Shed comprises designated spaces where elderly men can gather to work on community projects, through carpentry, woodworking and metalworking.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The things they make could even be sold, especially simple furniture pieces.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This is a step up from hanging around in the coffee shops, I mean elderly men drinking coffee and beer in the coffee shops.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: As elderly men spend their time and talents on useful pursuits, they will have a greater sense of achievement and can better contribute to the community.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: They will also make new friends and feel less lonely.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: With an ageing and increasingly well-educated population, there is a growing population of very competent and knowledgeable elderly whom we can tap on.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Examples are retired heads of Government agencies, retired principals and retired top executives from private organisations.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: With their wealth of experience, they will still have much to give in terms of leadership and mentorship.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I suggest that for those retirees who are keen to continue contributing, we can put in place a more formalised structure and clearer processes to facilitate the matching of their talents to organisations in need of it.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Allow me to summarise and conclude in Mandarin.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: (In Mandarin):  	We cannot change the fact of population ageing in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Hence, all of us must work together to allow our seniors to age peacefully.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The proposals put forward by the PAP.SG's team are comprehensive and insightful.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I wish to contribute an economic perspective to the problem of retirement adequacy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We inherited the CPF system from the British.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We have made it into one of the world's most comprehensive social security systems covering housing, retirement and health needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But we must understand that the fundamental design of the CPF system comes with strengths and weaknesses that today result in several urgent challenges for retirement adequacy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: One, there is a mismatch between earnings and expenditures in life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We are able to work in the earlier part of life but we face heavy financial burdens in the later part of life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A retirement policy must transfer money from the earning part to the later part of life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Two, there are retirement risks that individuals cannot protect themselves against.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot predict the number of our days or whether we will be in good health in retirement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot foresee what will be a good or bad investment decision.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The CPF system is what pension experts call a fully funded or defined contribution, individual account system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It fulfils the second pillar in the World Bank's "multi-pillar" model of pension systems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is fundamentally different from the other model of pay-as-you-go state pensions, which is the primary system in many European countries, and which is the first pillar in the World Bank model.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The difference is in how you provide money for retirement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In a funded system like CPF, each of us needs to invest enough money into our own individual account to draw on for retirement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But in a pay-as-you-go system, all that retirement money comes from taxes on the current working population.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The challenges facing retirees today under CPF are directly related to this difference in retirement system design.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The first challenge is basic retirement adequacy among the Pioneer Generation and the Merdeka Generation, that is, those who are already elderly today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is improving gradually, but we cannot expect this problem to go away in the near future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This problem is inherent to the design of a funded individual account system like CPF which transfers money from the working part of life to the retired part.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If there are insufficient savings during working life, there will be insufficient money in retirement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Now, this lack of money is not because of lack of thrift or lack of hard work in the Pioneer and Merdeka Generations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is because wages were much lower in the past and many never contributed to CPF because they worked in the informal sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Life expectancies and medical costs have also risen faster than expected.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: How does a pay-as-you-go system address these issues?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A pay-as-you-go pillar relies on taxation of the working population.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The flaw is that without enough adult workers, such a system cannot pay benefits sustainably.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, the importance of the old-age support ratio for such systems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But being able to tax current workers to pay for retirees means that you are not limited to the financial resources of only the previous generation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is what gives pay-as-you-go pillars the flexibility to make up for unforeseen changes to retirement costs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: That is, we could formally combine pay-as-you-go elements with the CPF individual savings scheme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We already have the Silver Support Scheme which is effectively a pay-as-you-go means-tested state pension.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The retirement payout should further be benchmarked to inflation or wages.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The problem we are concerned with is the elderly who are at the end of their working lives and who are facing the prospect of a hard retirement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The supplementary pension can be phased in based on the retirement or re-employment age, to encourage seniors to work if they are able to.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But once they pass a certain age, they should be taken care of without exception.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We can also structure the supplementary pension similar to the WIS scheme to fall as a CPF member's own retirement sum rises, but not so rapidly that it discourages work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We can also means-test the payout in the same way as other Government payouts, based on the person’s housing type or family support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Part of the financing will be coming from funds already committed to the Silver Support Scheme and Public Assistance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The benefit of integrating existing assistance schemes is that it makes the CPF system a one-stop shop for your retirement needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If the benefit amount is more generous than present levels, and it may need to be, then we will have to commit to additional Government expenditure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But I think we are too affluent today to have our elderly work because they have to, and not because they want to.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I hope we can ask Singaporeans to make a sacrifice so that unwanted work for the elderly is a thing of the past.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Next, we must deal with our younger cohorts who have a longer runway to retirement of two decades or more.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We must study whether decisions made today might harm retirement adequacy in the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Otherwise, our children would end up having the same discussion all over again in 20 years' time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: And again, this is a fundamental design issue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The first issue is low or inconsistent contributions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Some Singaporeans simply do not earn enough to contribute significant sums to CPF.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The CPF system, as with many pension systems, is designed for the workforce of the last century.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It assumes that a worker will have a lifetime of regular employment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There is no provision for those who are self-employed or those who are in the gig economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There is also no entitlement for those who exit the labour force to give of themselves as caregivers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Low contributions are only a problem because many low contributors also have low incomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, we cannot expect that their private savings will be sufficient.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, the best policy for low contributors is to raise their wages and ensure they have more consistent work, by keeping up with our efforts in education and skills training.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But where retirement policy is concerned, we should make contributions to CPF as universal as possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We should work towards making contributing for retirement mandatory even for the self-employed, as is the practice in many countries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But to do this, we must also make contributing worthwhile for the self-employed and the low income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We must face the reality that the CPF system is often more attractive to the high income, than the low income, simply because the rich do not miss having their CPF contribution money in hand.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is an excellent risk-free asset, but every dollar counts for low-income workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We must make CPF more attractive to the less well-off Singaporean, which may mean, reducing how generous CPF is to the rich.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: One way of doing so is to convert the current tax treatment of CPF contributions from a tax relief to a CPF credit instead.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Income tax relief is only worth something if you pay a high rate of tax.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This means that CPF contributions are effectively cheaper for high-income Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is nearly three times the annual cost of the Silver Support Scheme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Because tax relief would be cancelled, higher income workers would pay more in tax than the value of the credit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But the credit would significantly boost retirement adequacy for the broad lower- to middle-class.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The second reason for failure to save enough is low returns on CPF savings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: CPF rates are very competitive as risk-free rates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But they are below rates of return on risky assets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is not practical nor desirable to expect every CPF member to know how to invest.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, individual active investing is unlikely to be the solution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: By offering a simplified, low-risk, low-cost passive investment option, it will minimise transaction costs from active investing, which experts identify as a major reason for the underperformance of retail investors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It will also provide higher expected returns than the CPF system, although with some risk.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Government should roll out the LRIS as soon as possible, and ensure that, through competitive tendering and oversight, management expenses are minimised and the underlying investment instruments are well-diversified to manage risk.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But LRIS, by itself, is not for everyone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, the low income, who would benefit the most from a higher rate of return, are the least able to absorb any downside risk.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, I urge the Government to study limited protection for downside risk in LRIS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: One way of doing so is to structure returns, so that volatility increases gradually as the sum invested in LRIS grows.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Or it may be to guarantee the risk by pegging the CPF Special Account interest rate for, say, the first few tens of thousands of dollars, to the current enhanced rates, or to LRIS rates, whichever are larger.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This would expose the Government to some risk and expenditure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But it may be better to spend the money upfront, rather than later on the indigent elderly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The CPF system's strength is also its weakness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: CPF covers every aspect of social security, ranging from housing to retirement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: CPF has also been used to provide employment security by altering CPF contribution rates to keep Singaporean workers competitive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is a very fine thing to have so many needs provided for under one large policy umbrella.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But sometimes, what you need is more focus.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I suggest that the Government set up a dedicated watchdog of the CPF system's role in retirement adequacy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There are several significant risks that this watchdog could examine which are, at present, inadequately understood.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: And the changing nature of the family and the implications for intergenerational support, both in money and in time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We should not let that success blind us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Within the context of the current CPF system, there are many opportunities for reform that will strengthen retirement adequacy today and for future generations.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This will pose immense challenges to Singapore and Singaporeans in the future.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, with the correct approach, the ageing population may prove to be a boon to our nation, while we continue to care for their needs and to support their aspirations.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In order to allow for this to happen, I urge the Government to act fast and boldly.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is imperative that we transform our economy, built environment and lifestyles to allow Singaporeans to live purposeful and happy lives, especially in their golden years.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: They must take ownership and, together, champion sustainable policies, projects and programmes in the community.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: For the public sector, the Government should implement more pro-elderly policies.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Also, work should be expedited to provide an elderly-friendly built environment to encourage seniors to stay active and healthy.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: For the private sector, businesses can adopt more pro-elderly business practices to provide meaningful and respectable jobs.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: For the third P, the people sector, seniors should seek motivation to lead active, healthy and happy lives.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: As mentioned above, we must support the aspirations of the elderly.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: From my experience, the aspirations of the elderly may be broadly classified under three categories.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: First, to continue working in either full-time or part-time jobs; second, to retire and pursue hobbies and passions; and third, to volunteer their resources, expertise and time for causes they find meaningful.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The seven conditions are, first, experiencing positive moments and developing a sense of gratitude; second, pursuing a meaningful career and finding meaning in our work; third, developing good relationships with family and friends; fourth, contributing to the community and volunteering for meaningful causes; fifth, having adequate financial security; sixth, engaging in hobbies which promote mental health; and seventh, maintaining good physical and mental health.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: First, call to redesign jobs suitable for seniors.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Three years ago, Holland-Bukit Panjang Town Council redesigned its horticultural work processes to provide job opportunities for seniors.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Collaborating with our landscape contractor, we sought to improve the quality of services through introducing a performance-based contract approach.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Through this initiative, we were able to create new job opportunities for seniors to work as town gardeners in our estates.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is a case in point of how employment opportunities for our seniors may be mutually inclusive with achieving higher quality of service.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Seniors possess many years of work and life experiences and can make meaningful contributions at work if provided with the proper support and pace of working.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: While it is important to focus on productivity to enhance the competitiveness of our firms, it is not enough to simply focus on quantity; quality is equally important.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: They are also usually more careful and diligent.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This will enhance service quality in Singapore, and result in less abortive work due to carelessness.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: A shift in the mentality of employers in both the public and private sectors is due.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Work should be redesigned in order to allow younger and older employees to complement each other's strengths so that we may produce goods and services of high quality and bolster the competitive edge of our firms.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Over the last 18 years, North West CDC has been promoting healthy living among our residents.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Not only have the activities that these clubs run benefited residents.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: They have also supported volunteerism for 700 seniors who have become healthy living champions, instructors, coordinators and volunteers.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: More importantly, many of these seniors have made lasting friendships while maintaining a healthy lifestyle.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: At the same time, I wish to invite more seniors to volunteer to make a difference to building a better community.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Three, call to implement successful active ageing pilot projects in the community on a nationwide scale.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: First, Mr Louis Tay, aged 60, Chairman of Bukit Panjang Community Sports Club.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Over the last 18 years, Mr Tay and his team of volunteers have been organising weekly and monthly briskwalking sessions for Bukit Panjang residents.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Their passion and contributions have helped many seniors to stay fit and healthy.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Second, Miss Kho, 69 years old, is one of the fittest dancers in North West Dance Fit Club, befitting her status as a master dance fit instructor.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: She has been instrumental in helping North West Dance Fit Club to grow to its current level of success.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Although the profile and interests of seniors may differ depending on the locale, it is important that we develop a national framework and support programmes and projects which have shown success, such as the two mentioned above, to motivate seniors to continue pursuing their passions and strengthening communal bonds.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Government can aid in its set-up and match grants from private donors in order to raise enough funds.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Four, call to augment the elderly-friendly built environment.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: My next and final point will pertain to the built environment.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: First, we have completed three phases of construction of covered linkways and car drop-off points.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: These link our MRT stations, Light Rail Transit stations, town centres and bus stops to public estate blocks in Bukit Panjang Town.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In addition, we have also built covered linkways connecting blocks to one another and built drop-off porches.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: These covered linkways have improved the walkability of our town and encouraged residents to walk without letting weather conditions hamper their travel.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Second, we have implemented measures to aid in both horizontal and vertical mobility.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Horizontally, we have built barrier-free access (BFA) amenities, such as ramps and walkways, in the entire town.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Vertically, almost all our blocks are installed with elevators, granting access to every level.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Based on feedback, these BFA amenities have encouraged seniors, including those wheelchair-bound seniors, to lead active lifestyles, moving around town for breakfast sessions with their friends, chitchatting with their neighbours and making new friends through engaging in activities organised by grassroots and community organisations.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Therefore, it is crucial, especially with the backdrop of a rapidly ageing population, that we expedite the building of elderly-friendly infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: According to the United Nations' report entitled World Population Ageing 2013, "Population ageing is taking place in nearly all the countries of the world.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Ageing results from decreasing mortality, and, more importantly, declining fertility." The World Health Organization's concept of active ageing refers to the process of optimising opportunities for health, participation and security in order to enhance quality of life as people age.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: However, ageing need not cause worry or gloom.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: If we plan ahead, ageing can be a positive experience for all.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to highlight three areas of focus for today's Motion on Ageing with Purpose: (a) redefining ageing; (b) senior volunteerism; and (c) harnessing wisdom.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to cite a groundbreaking research published in the journal PLOS ONE in 2013.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Dr Sergei Scherbov, from the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis in Austria, led a project with New York's Stony Brook University looking at how life expectancy has increased over the years.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: He said: "What we think of as old has changed.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Age can be measured as time already lived or it can be adjusted taking into account time left to live.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: What we think of as old has changed over time, and it will need to continue changing in the future as people live longer, healthier lives.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Someone who is 60 years old today, he argues, is middle-aged.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: However, 200 years ago, a 60-year-old person would be considered a very old person." Traditional measures of age simply categorise people as "old" at a specific age, often 65.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Also, previous research by the team showed that the traditional definitions put many people in the category of "old" who have characteristics of a much younger people.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: For the study, the researchers compared the proportion of the population that was categorised as "old" using the conventional measure that assumes that people become "old" at age 65, and the proportion based on their new measure of age, which incorporates changes in life expectancy.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The results show that, as expected, a faster increase in life expectancy leads to faster population ageing when people are categorised as "old" at age 65, regardless of time or place.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: But surprisingly, they lead to slower population ageing when the new measures of ages are used.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: We have to ask ourselves if such a study is necessary in Singapore as well to redefine what ageing means.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: On volunteerism, having worked most parts of their lives, I have come across many seniors who want to give back to the community.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: They actively seek out volunteering opportunities that are aligned to their interests and areas of expertise.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to share a story from my experience in my non-profit organisation, Roses of Peace.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Three years ago, we had a significant number of seniors signing up to join as volunteers for our annual distribution of Roses with greetings of peace to promote inter-religious harmony in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: As organisers, we were caught by surprise as we were not expecting seniors to join a youth-focused initiative.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: When I spoke to several of the seniors and asked how they came to know about our initiative, most of them said they came to know about us through Facebook and some of them said from friends.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Surprised, I turned to the youths and asked them how they came to know about our initiative and they said from Instagram!

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: And if I may add, the seniors were more sporting than our youngsters.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: So, as an organisation, we decided to take in not just youth volunteers but also those who are youthful.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: We should also look at using social media platforms, such as Facebook and WhatsApp groups, to engage and organise volunteering opportunities for them.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: And we should pay greater attention to harnessing the collective wisdom of our seniors and promote intergenerational bonding.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, Dr William Wan, who is the General Secretary of the Singapore Kindness Movement, has written a book – and very timely, in fact – titled "Through the Valley: The Art of Living and Leaving Well".

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: It covers a compendious array of relevant issues related to active ageing.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In our nation, there are many ordinary seniors like him who have crystallised intelligence that come with age and experience.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: We, as a nation, must learn to leverage them for they have still much to offer and contribute.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Young people have fluid intelligence which must be complemented by crystallised wisdom which comes only from having been there and having done that.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: It is, therefore, important for our nation to respect the seniors in our midst and enlist their continuing participation in nation-building.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: By bringing the young and the seniors together, we can learn from each other and bridge the generational gap through intergenerational bonding by working on common projects like racial and religious harmony, amongst others.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: My generation is made up of digital natives and we can help our seniors to overcome their phobia of the digital world.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: We can create more opportunities for seniors to navigate the complex world of digital technology.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: With our fluid intelligence and their crystallised intelligence and wisdom, we can work hand-in-glove to innovate practice systems and to enhance the quality of life and to make our lives together safer and more secure.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, if we can bridge the generational gap today, we can promote the art of living well and leaving well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My speech today is focused on the Support for Caregivers Motion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Motion presents an opportunity for us to reaffirm one important pillar of our Shared Values – family as the building block of our nation – as caregivers are mostly drawn from the family or extended family.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is a point that was emphatically made by Dr Chia Shi-Lu in his speech in moving this Motion and with which I fully agree.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To me, the focus of the caregiver Motion is to acknowledge the important role caregivers play in taking care of their senior family members and identify meaningful ways to support them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the end, our family is strengthened and, in the process, our communities and nation are also strengthened.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There are many caregivers who deserve recognition for what they do.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wish to highlight the case of an exemplary caregiver who resides in Bukit Batok Single Member Constituency.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: His name is Mr Noorman bin Semar, 57 years of age.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He used to work as a forklift driver.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Not only that, he has two elder sisters who are both unwell.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: His elder sister, now 59, is suffering from a rare disease that affected her spine for the past 20 years, leaving her bedridden.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Her husband, unfortunately, divorced her when she became bedridden.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: His eldest sister, now 61, is suffering from psoriasis.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She suffers from arthritis, too, and her mobility is restricted and is unable to work.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Noorman decided not to get married and focus on taking care of his mother and his sisters.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He needed to carry, bathe, clothe, clean and feed his bedridden mother and sister.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He demonstrated to me how he carried his mother, using his arms, instead of tugging at the pyjamas at the hips of his mother's, as he did not want to unwittingly injure her.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He learnt how to administer injections, do dressings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He accompanied his mother for every visit to the hospital for treatment.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He refused to entertain the notion of getting his bedridden mother and sister admitted into homes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He said, "This is my duty." He said, "I told my mother, I am your son, do not have to feel embarrassed about me cleaning and bathing you.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I will look after you well." This encouraged his mother.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Her morale was lifted and, as a result, her life expectancy improved as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He also shared that he helped as a volunteer in a nursing home, cutting patients' hair.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Home took care of its patients well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But he noticed that even though the patients are taken care of well, they feel sad because they rather be at their home being taken care of by their own blood relatives.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And this is a point that Dr Chia Shi-Lu made.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He said that he changed his mother's position frequently so that the pressure on her skin will be evenly distributed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He used a fan to ensure that she does not perspire too much.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He did, however, acknowledge that it is not easy to take care of aged parents generally.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He said, in Malay, "Satu ibu boleh jaga sepuluh anak, Sepuluh anak belum tentu boleh jaga satu ibu.", that is, one mother can take care of 10 children, but it is not a given that 10 children can take care of one mother.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We must make sure that this does not become a reality.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Noorman is at peace now because he knew that he looked after her as well as he could over two decades.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: His focus now is on his two ailing sisters.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is humbling to hear about Mr Noorman and his example.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It would have been natural for him to get married, have children and send his mother to a home for institutionalised care.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He eschewed that in favour of taking care of his mother and siblings personally.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He did that out of love and affection.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He made significant personal sacrifices and remained steadfast and resilient in the face of many challenges.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As shared by the hon Members who spoke before me, there are certainly other Noormans in our society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And this Motion allows us to shine a spotlight on their work.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am glad to note that health institutions have been recognising and encouraging caregivers through presentation of awards and sharing of their stories annually.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Children, many of whom will form the next generation of caregivers, would also learn from their inspiring examples.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I suggest that these efforts to recognise these caregivers be scaled up.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These heroes and heroines must be held up as worthy examples for us to follow.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this way, we can entrench the important social values, such as filial piety.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We can do this at the community level through newsletters and community functions, too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Turning to the issue of support, before we instinctively think of Government support, I would suggest that it is equally important for our respective communities to build ecosystems of support for caregivers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This will have a strong signalling effect and help us build, indeed, a caring environment where residents can seek and obtain help from fellow residents and community partners.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is much we can do at the community level and hon Members have shared their examples, in particular, a noteworthy speech by Dr Lily Neo.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wish to share some examples from Bukit Batok.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In Bukit Batok, with the help of South West CDC, our community leaders have been fortunate to partner Caregivers Alliance Ltd to run training courses for residents who are caregivers to family members suffering from mental issues, such as dementia.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These residents would then form peer support groups to support one another emotionally.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These caregivers, I am told, find this as a very welcome resource.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We formed a group of volunteers who are known as "health peers".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They are specially trained by staff of NUHS.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These health peers make house calls on seniors or attend functions targeting seniors.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They then engage the seniors and focus on reinforcing health messages, such as proper exercise, proper eating, following medication and treatment schedules.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the process, they support caregivers in ensuring that their senior family members who are ailing comply with these health messages.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, there are some challenges that these community efforts face.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And one significant challenge is the inability to leverage patient data.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As mentioned earlier, the health peers go from door to door to see whether they can help the families.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, at times, it becomes a bit of a hit-and-miss affair.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would welcome the Government's comments on this suggestion because it would really be a win-win situation on the part of the patients, the caregivers, the Government, the community, if we can make it work and there could be leveraging of one another's resources.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the Government front, we already have existing programmes to help caregivers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hon Members have today made clarion calls for even more support in terms of CPF top-ups, financial top-ups, caregiver allowance, caregiver leave and so on.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These could have assisted Mr Noorman when he stopped working as a full-time forklift driver and worked as a security guard to take care of his mother and sisters.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do agree that more support can be given to caregivers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is a utilitarian basis to encourage more financial support for caregivers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This may mean less need to provide for institution-based care or subsidies associated with this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, there is a basis to assume that there could be some savings that could be channeled to caregivers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am chary, however, of adding on to financial burden without understanding the full implications.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But for me, the non-tangible benefit of strengthening the family and taking care of the well-being of the caregivers should also be borne in mind.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I welcome the views of the Government on what it considers to be a responsible approach in providing financial support for caregivers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Then, I introduced the "3G Village" that we aspire to have, one built with care and respect for all ages as everyone has a meaningful role in it.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In that, I made several suggestions on how we could embrace our seniors at the workplace and how we can provide meaningful social activities to prevent isolation amongst our seniors.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Apart from our seniors, I also noted there is a need to assist their caregivers who are important members of the ecosystem in enabling our seniors to age in place and lead active, healthy lives.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Further, in 2018's Motion on Support for Senior Citizens, I raised the need for proactive actions from all in the community – personal prevention to social activeness, senior-friendly townships to social care networks.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Like others in this House, we recognise it is time for us to work cohesively as a community towards achieving a country of active seniors.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Today, I wish to focus my speech around some practical challenges and give four suggestions that can assist different groups of seniors in their housing planning and for them to age in place.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In 2016, HDB flats made up 73% of Singapore's total housing stock.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This represents a significant proportion of home dwellers living in public housing.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As people age and have changing lifestyle needs, they will transit from one flat to another.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: While most people today are still able to manage their decision-making process, it is useful to take a precautionary outlook on future needs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Current statistics have shown that an estimated one-tenth of the people aged 60 and above have dementia in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Half of those aged 85 and older are already diagnosed with dementia.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: By then, not only will the seniors' ability to remember, judge or care for themselves deteriorate, it is unlikely that they can benefit from any housing schemes like downsizing to a smaller flat with the Silver Housing Bonus, lease buyback or subletting a room which, in the first place, we have designed all these with them in mind.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Further to health conditions, the growing trend of singles over the past 15 years, as shown in the General Household Survey conducted by the Singapore Department of Statistics, adds on to this challenge.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With shrinking family size, it is unclear whether these singles will have the necessary family support to care for them when they age.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But what is certain is that they do require some form of decision-making on their behalf if they become mentally incapacitated.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: At that stage, housing and funds become ever more critical to them.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The process can be simplified with some instructions similar in approach to appointing nominees for the CPF account.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As a start, the service can be offered to all seniors who make new flat transactions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Subsequently, this can be extended to home owners aged 50 and above with an existing flat.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This will benefit those who are singles and joint tenancy senior couples to prepare ahead without incurring hefty legal fees and also the complexity for their family in managing the process in future.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Two, review restrictions on CPF savings for housing needs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Many Singaporeans we know finance their housing needs with the usage of CPF savings.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This topic is pivotal to many seniors and, especially so for those from the lower-income group, who have been relying largely on their CPF to finance the mortgage loan.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The question, of course, remains how much CPF funds retirees can use for the purchase of flats without compromising their retirement funds.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This actually impacts two groups of seniors – the seniors who wish to downsize, and the other are younger families who wish to purchase the older flats.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: There are some seniors who wish to downsize and move closer to their children or siblings for a better care network as they age.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For these seniors, I would say, mostly 50 years and above, who have adequate CPF funds in their Ordinary Account (OA) and Retirement Account (RA) to fully pay for the next flat purchase.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This cap results in them having to take a loan.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The uncertainty of securing a full-time job is high at that age.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Some seniors are either not working or, at best, on a part-time work basis.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Thus, they typically encounter difficulty in obtaining a loan or have a lower loan quantum if they qualify.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It would be a relief if the seniors can fully pay off for the property and not be burdened by further mortgage at that age.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I must emphasise the point that I am making is not about raising or whether more CPF monies should actually be allowed for use for flat purchase, but rather, for those who have sufficient CPF monies, it is better for them to pay with CPF than taking a loan.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As we can imagine, having to worry about monthly mortgage payments or legal fees that ensued from defaulted payment for a shelter that will see them through old age is a tricky situation that warrants a nuanced assessment of what is more essential for them as retirement.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: While this is an option for seniors to age in place if they choose not to move, there are seniors who feel that the price value of the lease they are getting does not proportionately commensurate the value of the flat.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For one to feel empowered and age with dignity, they need to, first, have a place they can live in and feel at ease.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: And this place is one they can call home.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Regardless of whether they own or rent the place, it needs to provide comfort when they have little else to turn to.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I know much has been done on the ground.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As a matter of fact, I see it in my own constituency of how the different agencies, for example, HDB, MSF and VWOs, collaborate to put their best efforts in enabling the underprivileged seniors to have a place to live in, socialise and being cared for.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Some of these underprivileged seniors only wish to have peace of mind knowing they have a shelter to live and rest in.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It takes a whole of community to care for them.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But the first step of having a permanent shelter is more than a baby step for them.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Lastly, provision of innovative transportation mode in a private estate.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: While the public transport networks in the heartlands are better connected and provide easier access to commuters, the same cannot be said for those living in the private estates.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In today's context, one can say it is designed as such because more own private vehicles in the private estates and can afford other forms of transport.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But in the years to come and with the increased ageing population, accessibility becomes equally important whether they live in the heartlands or in the private estates.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With age, the probability of seniors who are still capable of driving and can afford a car will begin to decline.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In some private estates, the distance to commute from home to the nearest public transport point can be daunting for the seniors.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This is especially so for estates with many slopes, like the one I have, and those frail seniors may need to walk at least 20 minutes or more to reach the first bus stop.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: From policies to community efforts, if we all consciously plan and look ahead to adapt with the changing needs of our seniors, I am certain our collective efforts will be rewarded as we enjoy a country and home that respect, embrace and enable our seniors to age with dignity.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The population around the world is, indeed, ageing.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is primarily driven by two key trends – people are living longer than before, and birth rates are declining.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: An ageing population is a relatively new phenomenon since, for the most part of human history, the population has been youthful and life expectancy was shorter.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This, naturally, has significant implications for the country’s economic and social policies.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With fewer working adults to support a growing number of elderly, the potential tax revenue from income tax, for example, has fallen significantly during times when there is an urgent need to increase our social spending to cushion the impact of a greying population.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In recent years, a number of economic and social initiatives have been implemented to mitigate the impact of an ageing population.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In public housing, the extension of LBS to larger flats allowed more seniors to unlock the remaining value of their HDB flats and have a steady flow of retirement income while continuing to age in their own housing units.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To ensure our elderly can age gracefully within a vibrant community, Kampung Admiralty was designed as an integrated retirement community.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In healthcare, the introduction of CHAS, Pioneer Generation and the soon-to-be announced in detail Merdeka Generation packages should help to alleviate health cost in this area.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Apart from these policies, it is also important, via moral suasion, to convince the elderly of the need to stay healthy and connected, and to support them with targeted interventions.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And these are the two areas that I will be focusing on.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With retirement age set at 62 and re-employment age at 67, Singaporeans are, on average, spending 15.2 to 20.2 years of their life in retirement.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many people I spoke to have found those statistics troubling because it has never occurred to them that their mobility and lifestyle could be severely restricted in their old age.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Underlining these statistics is the important message that everyone needs to take ownership of their own health because we could end up suffering from some form of disability if we do not cultivate healthy living and healthy eating habits.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the course of our conversation, after reminiscing about old times, the conversation became a little bit bitter-sweet as we started to talk about our peers, many of whom had begun to develop what we call the lifestyle illnesses – diabetes, hypertension, high blood pressure, high cholesterol and so on.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The conversation then turned to those who had gone for operations for anterior and posterior cruciate ligament replacements and everything.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It got quite sober when we discovered that a few of our cohort actually already passed on as well from heart attacks, cancer and the like.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My friend then shared that he himself had undergone two bypasses and had a stroke, all before the age of 45.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This was very sobering and it explained why he looked like he had lost a lot of weight, which I was too polite to mention.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But the point I am making is that he had no children, married with a wife who was not working, and he has already begun to think about what is going to happen to him come 15 years' time when he is in his 60s should his health take a turn for the worse.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When he found that I will be speaking on this Bill, we parted with these words, he said, "Bro, you must make the point.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Don't wait till you are in your 60s.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Start to eat healthy, start to live healthy, make your preparations." And it is with that in mind that I want to make this point that it is never too early to inculcate healthy living habits.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Apart from spending time educating senior citizens of the need to have a healthy diet and an active lifestyle, targeted efforts must be made to reach out to those who are in the younger age brackets so that they, too, can understand the importance of making changes to their lifestyle early.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Let us not wait till we reach the 60s, but let us go further upstream, let us start earlier.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And to put in place a holistic multi-agency masterplan on how they can make changes to their lifestyle, if we can encourage our citizens to age healthily and develop good lifestyle habits that would build a healthy foundation for the future.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This would involve agencies, such as MOH, the Agri-Food and Veterinary Authority (AVA) or the soon-to-be Singapore Food Agency (SFA), HPB and even Sport Singapore, working together to promote the holistic concept of healthy living.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such a multi-agency strategy could also involve the Ministry of Education (MOE) emphasising introducing school curriculums that teach children the importance of a proper diet and having more outdoor physical education hours to promote fitness.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To top these suggestions off, I would also urge the Government Ministries and agencies to take the lead to promote better work-life balance by setting aside some time at the end of the workday, perhaps once or twice a week, so that their staff can be encouraged to begin the habit of exercising regularly.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we strive to become a smart nation, we need to find more ways to empower our senior citizens to adopt the usage of technology in their daily lives.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Based on the statistics collated by the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA), smartphones seem to be one of the easiest ways for senior citizens to get connected to technology.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this sense, NLB and PA would provide the hardware of creating physical spaces where the elderly could learn about technology while IHLs provide the software of teaching the elderly.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And, of course, we encourage the youths to also interact with our elderly as well.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also urge the Government to consider how it could, perhaps through IMDA, partner homegrown technology companies like Creative Technologies or Razer and the like, to develop and produce basic smartphones or similar devices with functional smart features like e-payment and Internet access for senior citizens.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These "uniquely Singaporean" elderly-friendly phones could also incorporate larger fonts and instructions and features in the major languages.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This would help our seniors transit into the digital era, as not every senior citizen is able to afford a smart device.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The provision of this smart phone will remove the cost of ownership as one of the potential roadblocks that might impede the adoption of smartphones among senior citizens.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Moving forward, it is crucial for us to identify pockets of opportunity for interventions and implement a holistic suite of programmes to tackle the problem in an integrative manner.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I mentioned earlier that Singapore is facing a demographic timebomb with regard to the challenge of our ageing population.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While a timebomb is dangerous, as we have seen in many movies, it only causes damage if it eventually explodes.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, let us all work together as one people, one nation to ensure that we are able to defuse this timebomb by ensuring that we take the right steps to manage and support our elderly in a manner that will allow them to age with dignity and grace.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Maybe we should consider replacing our tea breaks with a high-intensity interval training.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The senior at home is akin to a gem.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: If our society is a collective expression of individual homes, then our seniors must be a gem in our society as well.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They have vast life experiences, accumulating wisdom along the way.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Although they have worked hard, the reality is that not all will be able to enjoy retirement or their golden years.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Some may not enjoy the best of health, yet others have to be caregivers to their family members.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: And as we move this Motion in the House and discuss how we can continue to strengthen our support for our seniors, I would like to discuss, in particular, our support for seniors who are caregivers.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Many of them share with me a common fear of their loved ones being stranded when they eventually pass on.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This anxiety can undermine their mental and emotional well-being if they do not enjoy a wider family or community support.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Channel NewsAsia's "On the Red Dot" programme recently produced a series on the lives of three families who struggle against rare disabilities.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Like many Singaporeans, taking in the scenes of their daily living broke my heart, especially the story of 34-year-old Ms Zakiah.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Ms Zakiah suffers from Buerger's Disease, an incurable disease of the arteries and veins in the arms and legs.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It causes inflammation of the blood vessels, and she has lost her toes and fingers, except her thumbs.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In the case of Ms Zakiah, she has no choice but to rely on the help of her 68-year-old mother, Mdm Musliah.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The physical, emotional and financial stress that Mdm Musliah faces on a daily basis is overwhelming, to say the least.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This is one case and she is not alone.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They are also likely to neglect their own personal well-being, such as not seeking medical attention for themselves, or missing medical appointments because of their commitments at home.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: At the other end of the spectrum are our seniors who are single, with no children and minimal family support.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They are probably the most vulnerable part of society that we need to pay special attention to.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Elderly singles or those who have lost their partners may also have to cope with the possibility of social isolation and loneliness.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I believe there is scope for more to be done to help this group of seniors.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is important that we mobilise all resources on the ground to help keep a lookout and provide broader community support and awareness for isolated seniors and senior caregivers.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Our grassroots, VWO networks and agencies, such as the Silver Generation Office, should collaborate and share data, if possible, to enable better outreach to seniors.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In my experience, rental blocks are usually well taken care of by VWOs.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: However, the lower segment in the 3-room or 4-room flats, especially those who have resettled from kampungs and have not made much economic progress, are at a higher risk of not being aware of the help available.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This group of less educated families do not know much about Government schemes or caregiver relief programmes.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They fall between the cracks and, therefore, it is important for us to actively reach out to them.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Some seniors do not want to seek treatment or say they do not want to know if they have health issues.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: When I was a volunteer of the National University Hospital (NUH) MediFund Committee, social workers used to tell us that they needed to persuade seniors to seek treatment.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They were reluctant as they do not wish to burden their children even if it is a $50 medication.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Sometimes, a small knee problem without the right treatment and medication causes them to be wheelchair-bound over time and they lose their quality of life.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Lastly, more awareness of the plight of these families and the schemes available to them should be communicated.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: After the airing of the On the Red Dot episodes, Singaporeans from all walks of life rallied to offer help and support.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For many of us, this awareness would not have been made possible without the families’ sharing on such a public platform.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I would, therefore, like to take this opportunity to recognise the production team for their work and sensitivity in putting together this content.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: And perhaps Ministries can also put up a series on what are the schemes available to such families.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: There is no doubt the Singapore society is compassionate and kind.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This increased awareness can help us think of what we can do individually to help Singaporeans who are less fortunate.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It spurs us on to be more empathetic to our fellowmen.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For our senior caregivers, let us all exercise even greater empathy towards them and help them lessen their worries in their golden years.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As one of the last speakers, everything that needs to be said has already been said but let me share my thoughts nonetheless.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As our population ages, there are many ageing-related challenges that we need to address and plan ahead for, so that we are not caught in a situation where older Singaporeans find it difficult to age actively and meaningfully, or stay relevant, and where caregivers to elderly Singaporeans find that there is insufficient support in place to help them care for the seniors living amongst us.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have begun to put in place measures to help Singaporeans age actively and meaningfully whether through legislation, such as later retirement, re-employment or employment credits for employers to employ older Singaporeans, assistance packages, such as the Pioneer Generation Package and the upcoming Merdeka Generation Package, or through community-led initiatives, such as Active Ageing Programmes or initiatives led by the Silver Generation Office.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These measures are commendable and have been crafted and curated taking into consideration the concerns of both employees and employers.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, as with all things, there are still areas for improvement.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have spoken about this matter in this House before.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a Singaporean turns 55, their CPF contribution rate is drastically reduced by 11% overall.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have asked before for this CPF contribution rate to be restored to the current rate of 37% in total at age 54 and below, or, even if the CPF contribution rate is to be cut, it should be done progressively over several years, rather than a drastic 11% cut as you cross your 55th birthday.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Again, I have spoken about this matter in this House before.
